title: Laying quarry tiles in a sand and cement bed
subtitle: Bed unglazed clay floor tiles in a wet mortar base for a durable kitchen or utility floor
excerpt: How to lay unglazed quarry floor tiles in a traditional sand and cement mortar bed. Covers mixing the bed, setting out the tiles, laying and tapping level, grouting with a cement slurry, and sealing.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1880s, public domain). Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for traditional tile laying.

glossaryTerms.definition: An unglazed dense clay floor tile, typically 150 x 150 mm or 225 x 225 mm and 12 to 20 mm thick, fired at high temperature. More porous than porcelain but extremely durable. Standard UK kitchen, utility, and farmhouse floor tile. Must be sealed after laying to prevent oil and grease absorption.

A mixed layer of sharp sand and cement laid over the floor substrate, screeded level, and used as the bedding layer for heavy floor tiles. Typically a 4:1 or 5:1 sharp sand to cement ratio by volume, mixed damp but not wet, known as a semi-dry mix.

content.text: give a floor that takes heavy use and last for generations. The bed is a semi-dry mortar mix, compacted roughly level under each tile, with the tile tapped down to the precise final level. Grouting uses a neat cement slurry rather than a pre-mixed grout.

The base must be solid concrete or a sound screed, free from cracks, high spots, and dust. Sweep and vacuum. Wet the floor thoroughly with clean water and allow to drain but not to dry out; a slightly damp base helps the mortar bed bond. Prime any dusty or very porous areas with an SBR (styrene-butadiene rubber) bonding agent diluted 1:3 with water and allow to become tacky before laying.

Find the centre of the room by snapping chalk lines between the midpoints of opposite walls. Dry-lay a row of tiles from the centre to each wall with a 10 mm gap between tiles, and check the cut sizes at each end. Aim for a cut larger than half a tile at every wall. If the layout gives a small sliver at one wall, shift the starting point by half a tile in that direction.
Mix and lay the mortar bed

Mix sharp sand and cement at 4:1 by volume (4 parts sharp sand, 1 part ordinary Portland cement) with just enough water to make a damp but not wet mix. The mix is right when you can squeeze a handful and it holds its shape without releasing water. Lay the mix to a depth of about 40 mm in a working area of around 1 square metre, screed it roughly level with a straight-edge, and tamp it down firmly.

Soak the quarry tiles in clean water for at least 30 minutes before laying. A dry tile draws moisture from the bed too quickly and weakens the bond. Apply a thin slurry coat of neat cement to the back of each tile (a cement wash, not a thick layer). Place the tile onto the bed and tap it down with a rubber mallet or the handle of a brick trowel until it is level with the surrounding tiles. Check level with the spirit level in both directions after every three or four tiles.

Allow the bed to harden for at least 24 hours before grouting. Mix neat cement with water to a thick cream consistency and brush it into the joints with a stiff brush, working it fully in. Sweep excess from the tile faces with a damp cloth before it sets. For a darker joint colour, add a small amount of dark pigment to the grout slurry. Leave the grout to harden for two to three days before walking on the floor.

Allow the floor to cure for a minimum of two weeks before sealing. Apply two coats of a penetrating quarry tile sealer with a brush or lint-free cloth, allowing the first coat to dry fully before applying the second. The sealer closes the pores in the unglazed clay and prevents oil and grease from staining the surface permanently.
A 45-degree diagonal layout gives the same tile a different character and makes a small room appear larger. The centre-of-room setup is the same; the tiles are simply rotated 45 degrees.
A black and white chequered floor uses two coloured quarry tiles in the same bed method. Sort the tiles by shade before laying: quarry tiles vary batch to batch.

attrs.symptom: Tiles hollow-sound and rock when walked on after setting
attrs.cause: Air pockets under the tile because the bed was not compacted evenly, or the tile back was not slurry-coated.
attrs.fix: Lift the hollow tile while the bed is still fresh enough to rework. Compact the bed, re-slurry the tile back, and re-lay. Once the bed is fully hard, hollow tiles need cutting out with an angle grinder.

attrs.symptom: White efflorescence appears on the tile surface after a few weeks
attrs.cause: Soluble salts in the cement bed migrating through the porous tile as moisture evaporates.
attrs.fix: Brush off with a stiff brush and allow the floor to dry fully. Seal the floor once the efflorescence stops recurring.

attrs.symptom: Tiles lifting at the edges or corners
attrs.cause: The mortar bed dried too quickly before the tile bonded, or the tiles were not soaked before laying.
attrs.fix: Soak replacement tiles for longer before relaying. In hot weather, keep the laid area damp with a damp cover for 24 hours.
